# Volume 1 — CHAPTER V. Nell’s History

!!! note "Source text"
    Passages cited on the wiki pages link into this page. Only volumes at or before
    this page's cutoff are present.

“DO you know,” Nell remarked in confidence, “I have decided that I will enjoy this drive. Experience has taught me that if a person firmly resolves to enjoy things, they almost always can. Naturally, one has to resolve it firmly. While this drive is happening, I intend not to dwell on returning to the asylum. My thoughts will be focused solely on the drive. Oh, see, a single early wild rose has bloomed over there! Is it not beautiful? Wouldn't you agree that it must be happy being a rose? Wouldn't it be wonderful if roses were able to speak? I am certain of their ability to share such wonderful things with us. And isn't pink the absolute most charming hue anywhere? I adore it, yet it doesn't suit me. Pink cannot be worn by individuals with red hair, even inside their imagination. Have you ever heard of someone who had red hair during childhood, but whose hair turned into a different shade upon reaching adulthood?”
{: #nw-v01-c05-p0000 }

“No, I cannot say that I ever have,” Thirza remarked without pity, “and I doubt that such a thing will occur for you either.”
{: #nw-v01-c05-p0001 }

A sigh escaped Nell.
{: #nw-v01-c05-p0002 }

“Well, another expectation has been shattered. ‘My life is a perfect graveyard of buried hopes.’ Having come across that line in a book one time, I repeat it to console myself each time I face disappointment about something.”
{: #nw-v01-c05-p0003 }

“I fail to perceive the comfort in it myself,” Thirza remarked.
{: #nw-v01-c05-p0004 }

“Well, it is due to how lovely and romantic it sounds, precisely as though I were a book's heroine, don't you see. Romantic things appeal to me deeply, and what could be more romantic than a graveyard packed with interred hopes, don't you think? Having one actually pleases me quite a bit. Will our journey take us over the Lake of Glassy Waters today?”
{: #nw-v01-c05-p0005 }

“If your Lake of Glassy Waters refers to Pembroke’s pond, that is not our route. Our path lies along the shore road.”
{: #nw-v01-c05-p0006 }

“The shore road sounds lovely,” Nell remarked in a dreamy voice. “Does its beauty match its name? The moment you mentioned ‘shore road’, a mental image of it appeared to me, just like that! Pale Sands is also a charming name; however, I do not prefer it to Brierley. Brierley is a beautiful name that resembles music when heard. What is the distance to Pale Sands?”
{: #nw-v01-c05-p0007 }

“The distance is five miles; since you are clearly determined to converse, you may just as well speak to some end by informing me of what you know concerning your own history.”
{: #nw-v01-c05-p0008 }

“Oh, the things I know regarding myself are not actually worth mentioning,” Nell stated with enthusiasm. “Should you merely allow me to describe my self-imagined ideas, you will find it far more fascinating.”
{: #nw-v01-c05-p0009 }

“No, I have no desire for any of your imaginings. You must merely adhere to plain facts. Start right at the start. Where did your birth take place and what is your age?”
{: #nw-v01-c05-p0010 }

“I turned eleven this past March,” Nell stated, giving in to plain reality with a faint sigh. “And Nova Scotia’s Harborough is where I was born. Edmund Harcourt was my father’s name, and he worked as a teacher at the Harborough High School. Bertha Harcourt was my mother’s name. Don’t you think Edmund and Bertha are beautiful names? I feel so happy that my parents possessed pleasant names. Having a father who was named—oh, for instance Jedediah—would be an actual shame, wouldn’t it?”
{: #nw-v01-c05-p0011 }

“It likely is not important what an individual is called provided that he conducts himself properly,” Thirza stated, believing she was required to teach a helpful and virtuous lesson.
{: #nw-v01-c05-p0012 }

“Well, I don’t know.” Nell seemed to be pondering. “A book I once read stated that a rose would smell just as sweet if it had a different name, but believing that has always been impossible for me. A rose would not be as lovely if it were named a thistle or a skunk cabbage, in my opinion. Even if my father had been named Jedediah, I imagine he could still have been a fine man; however, I am certain it would have proved a burden. Well, my mother was also a High School teacher, but naturally, she relinquished her teaching career upon marrying father. Managing a husband was a sufficient duty. They were a couple of infants and as poor as church mice, according to Mrs. Thomas. They moved into a tiny little yellow house located in Harborough. Although I have never set eyes on that house, it has been in my imagination thousands of times. It surely had honeysuckle climbing over the parlor window, lilacs growing in the front yard, and lilies of the valley right by the gate, I believe. Yes, and every window had muslin curtains. Muslin curtains bestow such a grand feel upon a house. My birth occurred in that very house. Mrs. Thomas remarked that I was the ugliest infant she had ever laid eyes on, being extremely thin, small, and composed of nothing but eyes, yet mother considered me utterly gorgeous. A mother ought to be a superior judge compared to a poor woman who arrived to perform scrubbing, wouldn't you agree? At any rate, I am pleased she felt contented with me; it would bring me great sorrow to think I disappointed her—since her life ended shortly after that, you understand. Fever took her life when my age was merely three months. I truly wish her life had lasted long enough for me to possess a memory of addressing her as mother. Saying ‘mother’ would be so lovely, don't you think? Then, four days later, fever caused father's death as well. Consequently, I became an orphan, and people were utterly baffled, as Mrs. Thomas recounted, regarding how to handle me. As you can tell, no one desired me even at that time. It appears to be my destiny. Places far off were the origins of both father and mother, and it was common knowledge that they possessed no living relatives. In the end, Mrs. Thomas announced she would accept me, despite her poverty and her intoxicated husband. I was brought up by hand by her. Is there any quality in being brought up by hand that should render individuals raised in that manner superior to others, do you happen to know? For every time I behaved badly, Mrs. Thomas would inquire, in a reproachful manner, how I could turn out to be such a wicked girl when she had brought me up by hand.
{: #nw-v01-c05-p0013 }

“Mr. and Mrs. Thomas relocated from Harborough to Marysville, and I remained in their household until my eighth year. My duties included helping to care for the Thomas children—four of whom were my juniors—and they certainly required a great deal of attention, I assure you. Following Mr. Thomas’s fatal accident when he fell beneath a train, his mother proposed to harbor Mrs. Thomas and the young ones, though she refused to accept me. Mrs. Thomas expressed that she was utterly bewildered as to how to dispose of me. At that juncture, Mrs. Rudge traveled down from further up the river and offered to adopt me, owing to my skill with young ones, whereupon I journeyed upriver to reside with her in a modest clearing surrounded by stumps. The location was exceedingly desolate. Had I lacked an imagination, I am positive I could not have endured staying there. Mr. Rudge operated a small sawmill at that site, while Mrs. Rudge was the mother of eight children. On three separate occasions, she gave birth to twins. Although I am fond of infants in reasonable numbers, bearing twins thrice consecutively exceeds proper bounds. I stated this to Mrs. Rudge with conviction when the final set arrived. Lugging them around used to exhaust me so terribly.
{: #nw-v01-c05-p0014 }

“For more than two years, I resided up river alongside Mrs. Rudge, but after Mr. Rudge passed away, Mrs. Rudge dissolved her household. Following the distribution of her children among her family members, she departed for the States. Since no one was willing to receive me, I was forced to enter the asylum located at Marden. Even the asylum did not desire my presence, claiming they were already experiencing overcrowding. Nevertheless, they were obligated to admit me, and I remained in that place for four months until the arrival of Mrs. Tranter.”
{: #nw-v01-c05-p0015 }

Nell concluded her remarks with a further sigh, which now expressed relief. Clearly, discussing her encounters within a world where she had been unwelcome was not to her liking.
{: #nw-v01-c05-p0016 }

“Was school ever somewhere you went?” asked Thirza, steering the sorrel mare onto the coastal road.
{: #nw-v01-c05-p0017 }

“Hardly anything. During my final year residing with Mrs. Thomas, I attended for a short time. After moving up river, the school was located at such a distance that winter walking was impossible, and summer brought vacation, leaving me able to attend solely throughout the spring and autumn months. Naturally, I attended during my stay at the asylum, though. Reading comes quite easily to me, and I have memorized a great number of poems—‘The Battle of Hohenlinden’ along with ‘Edinburgh after Flodden,’ as well as ‘Bingen on the Rhine,’ plus numerous selections from ‘Lady of the Lake’ and the majority of James Thompson’s ‘The Seasons.’ Are you not simply fond of poetry that causes a tingling sensation along your spine? A poem featured in the Fifth Reader—‘The Downfall of Poland’—is absolutely packed with excitement. Naturally, my placement was not in the Fifth Reader—I had only reached the Fourth—yet the older girls would allow me to borrow their copies for reading.”
{: #nw-v01-c05-p0018 }

Glancing sideways at Nell, Thirza inquired, “Were those women—Mrs. Thomas and Mrs. Rudge—good to you?”
{: #nw-v01-c05-p0019 }

“O-o-o-h,” Nell stammered. A deep red wash instantly covered her delicate small face, and her forehead displayed her discomfiture. “Oh, their intentions were—I am certain their intentions were to be as friendly and gentle as they could be. And if folks intend to treat you well, you are not overly bothered if they are not entirely—at all times. They had many troubles to upset them, as you are aware. Having a spouse who drinks is extremely difficult, as you can understand; and having three consecutive sets of twins must be terribly difficult, wouldn’t you agree? Even so, I am certain their intention was to treat me well.”
{: #nw-v01-c05-p0020 }

Thirza ceased her questioning. Nell surrendered to mute delight regarding the coastal route, and Thirza drove the sorrel in an absent-minded fashion as she thought intently. Compassion was abruptly awakening in her soul toward the young girl. What a deprived, loveless existence she had endured—an existence marked by hard labor, indigence, and disregard; because Thirza possessed sufficient acumen to discern what lay beneath the surface of Nell’s past and grasp the reality. It was no surprise that she had felt such joy when considering a true home. It was unfortunate that her return was necessary. What would happen if she, Thirza, were to humor Obed’s inexplicable desire and allow her to remain? He was determined about the matter; and the young girl appeared to be a pleasant, impressionable small person.
{: #nw-v01-c05-p0021 }

“She speaks far too much,” Thirza reflected, “though that habit could perhaps be corrected. Furthermore, her speech contains nothing vulgar or colloquial. Her manners are refined. Her family was probably respectable.”
{: #nw-v01-c05-p0022 }

The coastal route was “woodsy and wild and lonesome.” Dense scrub firs, whose vigor remained completely unbowed by decades of fighting the gulf gales, lined the right side. On the left stood the sheer red sandstone bluffs, which approached the path so closely at points that a horse with less calm than the sorrel could have unsettled the passengers she pulled. At the foot of the bluffs rested piles of wave-eroded stones or small sand inlets set with pebbles like sea gems; past them stretched the ocean, glinting and azure, while overhead flew the gulls, their wings gleaming like silver in the sun’s rays.
{: #nw-v01-c05-p0023 }

“Is the sea not marvelous?” asked Nell, breaking a lengthy, staring quietness. “A single time, back when Marysville was my home, Mr. Thomas rented a delivery wagon and escorted every one of us to pass the day by the coast ten miles distant. Every second of that day brought me delight, despite my having to care for the kids the entire time. For years afterward, I re-experienced it in joyful dreams. However, this coastline surpasses the Marysville coastline. Are those gulls not magnificent? Would being a gull appeal to you? I believe it would to me—meaning, provided I was unable to be a human girl. Do you not agree that waking at dawn, swooping down toward the waves, and traveling far across that beautiful blue all day would be wonderful; and subsequently returning to one’s nest at night? Oh, I am able to picture myself doing that very thing. What large dwelling is that directly before us, if you don’t mind?”
{: #nw-v01-c05-p0024 }

“Over there is the Pale Sands Hotel. It is operated by Mr. Kirke, though the season is not under way yet. A great number of Americans arrive at that place for the summer. This coast is considered by them to be ideal.”
{: #nw-v01-c05-p0025 }

“I feared it could be the home of Mrs. Tranter,” Nell stated sorrowfully. “Reaching that destination is something I wish to avoid. In a way, it will feel as though all things have come to a close.”
{: #nw-v01-c05-p0026 }
